title.en: Concurrency theorems of Ceva and Menelaus

text.en: When do three lines drawn from the vertices of a triangle meet at one point? Giovanni Ceva gave a simple test in 1678.

A cevian is a line segment from a vertex of a triangle to the opposite side; medians, altitudes and angle bisectors are special cevians.
Ceva's theorem: cevians AD, BE, CF are concurrent if and only if BD/DC times CE/EA times AF/FB equals 1.
Medians are concurrent because each ratio equals 1; the point of concurrence is the centroid.
Menelaus theorem: points P, Q, R on the sides BC, CA, AB are collinear if and only if BP/PC times CQ/QA times AR/RB equals -1 for directed lengths.
With ordinary lengths the product for collinear points is 1.
Ceva is used to show that the angle bisectors, medians and altitudes are concurrent.

problem.en: In triangle ABC, AB = 13, AC = 14, BC = 15. Points D, E, F lie on BC, CA, AB with AF/FB = 2/5 and CE/EA = 5/8. If AD, BE, CF are concurrent, find BD and DC.

text.en: So BD = 4 DC. Also BD + DC = 15.

prompt.en: Trees P, Q, R are on lines BC, AC, AB with BP = 2, PC = 6, CQ = 3, QA = 5, RA = 10, RB = 2. Are they collinear?

requiredIdeas.en: The product is 1, so by Menelaus they are collinear

points.en: Ceva: product of three ratios = 1 for concurrency.
Centroid is the meeting point of medians.
